title: Act II, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: Alone in his orchard at night, Brutus decides Caesar must die, not for what he has done but for what he might become: 'think him as a serpent's egg.' He reads a forged letter urging him to act. The conspirators arrive; Brutus refuses an oath, refuses to include Cicero, and overrules Cassius's plan to kill Antony too: 'Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers.' Decius promises to bring Caesar to the Capitol. Portia, who has wounded her own thigh to prove her constancy, demands to share his secret. Ligarius, though sick, joins.

annotationFocus.passage:
The exhalations whizzing in the air
Give so much light that I may read by them. Opens the letter and reads.
“Brutus, thou sleep’st: awake, and see thyself.
Shall Rome, etc. Speak, strike, redress!
Brutus, thou sleep’st: awake!”
Such instigations have been often dropp’d
Where I have took them up.
“Shall Rome, etc.” Thus must I piece it out:
Shall Rome stand under one man’s awe? What, Rome?
My ancestors did from the streets of Rome
The Tarquin drive, when he was call’d a king.
“Speak, strike, redress!” Am I entreated
To speak and strike? O Rome, I make thee promise:
If the redress will follow, thou receivest
Thy full petition at the hand of Brutus!

words.sentence:
We all stand up against the spirit of Caesar;
And in the spirit of men there is no blood:
O, that we then could come by Caesar’s spirit,
And not dismember Caesar!

Seek none, conspiracy;
Hide it in smiles and affability:
For if thou path, thy native semblance on,
Not Erebus itself were dim enough
To hide thee from prevention.

Dwell I but in the suburbs
Of your good pleasure?

Our course will seem too bloody, Caius Cassius,
To cut the head off and then hack the limbs,
Like wrath in death and envy afterwards;
For Antony is but a limb of Caesar:
Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Portia proves her 'constancy' by showing a 'voluntary wound / Here, in the thigh' she gave herself.
